unit.title: Apply the principles of customer service

summary: This unit teaches you the principles of good customer service in a villa, hotel, restaurant or attraction: why service matters to guests, the business and Jamaica, how to present yourself and speak to guests, how to look after them through the guest cycle, how to share honest product and local knowledge, how to serve guests with different needs, and how to put things right when service goes wrong.

blocks.p: Customer service is how you treat the people your business serves. In tourism, those people are **guests**, and how they feel when they leave decides whether they come back, tell their friends, and write a good review. Rooms, food and scenery matter, but guests remember **people**.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It applies to every job: the gardener who greets a guest, the cook who checks an allergy, the room attendant who leaves a room perfect, the front desk agent on the telephone. Good service is everyone's job.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper with multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays, and two group practical tasks. In the first you role-play guest cards in the mock villa: welcome, welcome drink, luggage, finding out needs, a special request, goodbye, and a guest history card. In the second you make a guest information sheet and answer guest questions at a mock tour desk, including an email reply. Use made-up names and details.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In role plays, serve non-alcoholic drinks only, wash your hands before touching glasses, carry trays safely and lift luggage with your knees bent and your back straight.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: What customer service is, and why it matters

head: Topic
Product
Service
rows: What it is
What the guest buys and can see or touch
How the guest is treated while buying and using it
Restaurant example
The jerk chicken: its taste, portion and price
The greeting, the speed, the smile, how the server answers questions
Villa example
The room, the pool, the view
The welcome, the clean room, the way requests are handled

blocks.p: Two properties can sell the same room at the same price. The one with the better **service** wins the guest's return visit.

ul: A guest's **expectations** come from the property's website and photos, online reviews, what friends say, the price and past stays.
If the service is **below** expectations, the guest feels let down and may not come back, and may tell others.
If it **meets** them, the guest is satisfied. If it is a little **above**, the guest is delighted. That is the aim.

head: Kind of need
Meaning
Examples
rows: Physical
What the body needs to be comfortable and safe
A cold drink on a hot day
A clean, cool room and a comfortable bed
Safe, tasty food
Emotional
How the guest feels
To feel welcome and valued
To feel safe and respected
To feel that someone cares

blocks.p: Good service meets both. A perfect room is not enough if the guest feels ignored.

ul: **For the guest**: a happy stay.

**For the business**: satisfied guests return and recommend the property. Repeat guests cost less to win than new ones and bring steady income. This is **word of mouth**. Poor service brings complaints, refunds and bad reviews.
**For you**: guests who are happy are easier to work with. Good service builds your reputation and your promotion chances.

**For Jamaica**: tourism earns foreign exchange and provides many jobs, directly and indirectly. When visitors are welcomed warmly, they come back, which supports farmers, fishers, craft makers, drivers and many others.

blocks.p: **Every** member of staff, in every department, from the gardener to the manager. Staff who deal with guests face to face are **front-line staff**: servers, front desk agents, bell staff, tour guides. But front-line staff depend on those behind the scenes: cooks, housekeepers, maintenance.
Each time a guest has contact with the business, they form an opinion. These are **moments of truth**: the greeting, the first look at the room, the reply to an email, the bill. Get them all right.

blocks.note: Team Jamaica is training in welcoming visitors and showing the best of Jamaican hospitality. It is run by the Tourism Product Development Company (TPDCo). Ask your instructor how to take part.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Your co-workers are your **internal customers**. When the kitchen cooks a dish quickly and correctly, the server can serve it well. When housekeeping reports a room ready, the front desk can check in a guest. Treat colleagues politely, pass on information clearly and help each other, because the guest feels the whole team.

sections.title: Presentation, attitude and the way you speak

blocks.p: Guests judge you within seconds, by what they see and hear. A neat, willing worker makes guests feel looked after before a word is spoken.

head: Do
Avoid
rows: Shower daily; clean, pressed uniform; clean shoes; name badge
Wearing your own clothes because the uniform is in the wash
Hair neat and, for food service, tied back or covered
Strong perfume or cologne
Short, clean nails
Lots of rings, bracelets and chains
Clean hands, washed often
Eating, chewing gum or using your phone in front of guests

ul: Stand up straight, face the guest, smile and make eye contact.
Keep your hands out of your pockets and do not lean on the counter or wall.
Do not look at your phone, look around the room, sigh or fold your arms.
Leave a comfortable space between you and the guest.
Be positive and willing: greet warmly, stay calm when it is busy, and offer help without being asked.
Give the same care at the end of a long shift as at the start.
Do not sigh, argue or look bored. Even a good room or meal feels poor to a guest who has been treated badly.
Give every guest the same high standard, whether or not they tip, and whatever they look like or wear.
Use **title and surname**, such as 'Mrs Grant' or 'Mr Williams', once you know the name. Do not use a pet name, a nickname you made up, or a room number.
Use a **warm, calm, polite tone**. Speak clearly and not too fast. Do not be loud or sharp.
Use plain words. Avoid slang and short forms that guests from other countries may not understand.
Listen first. Do not interrupt, finish the guest's sentences or talk to a co-worker while a guest is waiting.

blocks.p: Tell the guest what you **can** do, not only what you cannot.

head: Instead of
Say
rows: 'No, that's finished.'
'I'm sorry, the fish is finished tonight, but the jerk chicken is very popular. Would you like to try it?'
'You can't check in until three.'
'Your room will be ready by 3 p.m. Until then you are welcome to relax by the pool, and we can keep your bags safe.'
'That's not my department.'
'I'll find out who can help and I will make sure they come to you.'
'I don't know.'
'Let me find out for you.'

blocks.p: Even when you must say no, a calm, polite and **firm** tone shows respect. Offer a choice so that the guest still feels looked after.

sections.title: Communicating with guests: face to face, telephone and email

flow: Greet the guest within a few seconds, with a smile
Use their name if you know it
Ask open questions to find out what they want
Listen carefully and show that you have understood
Give clear, correct information
Check that they have what they need
Thank them

ul: If you are busy with one guest when another arrives, **acknowledge** the new guest with a smile or a nod and say 'I'll be with you in a moment'. Do not make them feel ignored.
Ask open questions, such as 'What kind of food do you like?' and 'How much would you like to spend?', so you can match your suggestions to the guest. Do not guess.
Repeat orders or requests back to the guest to check them.
Answer quickly, within a few rings. Greet, give the name of the property and your own name, and ask 'How may I help you?'
**Smile** when you speak. Callers cannot see you, but a smile can be heard in your voice.
Have a pen and paper ready. Write down names, numbers and messages, and repeat them back.

Ask before you put a caller on hold, and wait for their answer. Do not leave them on hold for long. If the person they want is still busy, go back, explain and offer to take a message or arrange a call-back.
Do not transfer a call without telling the caller where it is going.
Thank them for calling, and let the caller hang up first.
Reply to emails **promptly**, the same day if you can. A reply a week later is poor service.
Use a greeting, a clear and polite answer, accurate times and prices, and a sign-off with your name.
Use plain, correct English. Do not use text-message short forms or capital letters (they look like shouting).
Check names, dates and amounts before you send. Confirm bookings and special requests **in writing**.

blocks.p: When a guest asks for something you cannot do yourself, take responsibility for it: say who will help, tell the guest roughly when, pass the message clearly (write it in the log) and check that it was done. A guest should not have to ask twice.
The **guest cycle** is the stages a guest goes through from booking to leaving, and afterwards. Good service at every stage creates a smooth, happy stay.

head: Stage
What the guest needs
Good service
rows: Before arrival
Information, a booking and confidence
A prompt, polite reply with clear prices and details
A written confirmation
Ask about special needs: a baby cot, a food allergy, an arrival time, an anniversary
Offer airport transfers, if available
Arrival
To feel welcome; to settle in
Greet by name with a smile
Offer a **welcome drink** (a cool, non-alcoholic fruit punch or water)
Help with the luggage
Explain the property and its services, house rules and emergency exits
Make check-in quick, especially for tired guests after a long flight
The stay
A clean, comfortable, safe stay and quick help
Keep rooms and public areas clean
Deal with requests promptly
Give honest advice on local tours and beaches
Notice and meet needs before the guest asks
Departure
A correct bill; an easy exit
Have the bill ready and correct, explain any charges
Help with luggage and the taxi
Thank the guest, wish them a safe trip and invite them back
After the stay
To feel remembered
Record the guest's likes on a **guest history card**
Send a thank-you message
Welcome them back next time, using what you recorded

ul: To **anticipate** a need is to notice what a guest will need and offer it before they ask. Examples: bringing a high chair when a family with a baby arrives; putting out extra towels when guests return from the beach; offering a cold drink to a hot, tired guest.

To **exceed expectations** is to give a little more than the guest expected, so that they are pleasantly surprised. Examples: leaving a card and fresh fruit for an anniversary couple; remembering a returning guest's favourite drink.

Both have **limits**. Anything that costs money or changes the rules needs your supervisor's approval. Respect privacy: a birthday is not for announcing to other guests. Never promise what the property cannot deliver.

blocks.p: A guest history card or record notes the guest's past stays and likes: room preference, favourite food and drink, special dates, allergies. It lets the next member of staff serve the guest better. Keep it private and accurate, and use it only to improve service.

sections.title: Product knowledge, local knowledge and payments

blocks.p: Guests expect staff to answer questions at once. Learn the facts, and keep a printed information sheet within reach.

head: A guest might ask
You should know
rows: What time is breakfast? When does the pool close?
Opening times of the restaurant, bar, pool, spa and gift shop
Is there Wi-Fi?
How to connect, and the password
Which dishes have no nuts or no pork?
The menu, the ingredients, and whom to ask in the kitchen
How much is breakfast, or a tour?
Prices, what is included and what is extra
Can I get a late check-out?
The policy, and whom to ask

blocks.p: If you do not know, **say so and find out**, then go back quickly. Never guess: a wrong answer wastes the guest's time and can put them at risk.

ul: Distances and directions to the nearest beach, pharmacy, bank, shop and attractions; taxi fares to the airport; emergency numbers.
Give clear directions, a map and the travel time. Do not just point and say 'over there'.
Recommend only **licensed or approved** tour operators, guides and taxis that the property uses. Do not send guests to someone who simply offers a cheap ride or tour on the beach.
Give **honest** information about safety: if the sea has strong currents, warn the guest and suggest a safer spot or a lifeguarded beach. If a trail is closed or the weather is poor, say so.
Know any age, weight or health limits on tours, and explain them kindly.

blocks.p: Suggesting extras helps the guest and the business, as long as it is polite and honest. 'Would you like a glass of fresh sorrel with that?' is a suggestion. 'You have to order a drink' or 'Everybody here orders the most expensive wine' is pressure. Match suggestions to what the guest has told you, and never push.

ul: Prices may be in J$ or US$. When a guest pays in a different currency from the price, use the **exchange rate the property has set for that day**, not one you heard or one the guest suggests.

**GCT** (General Consumption Tax) is added to many bills at the current rate. If a guest asks why the bill is higher than the menu prices, explain politely that taxes, and a service charge where the property has one, are added. Check your property's policy.
Some properties do not allow staff to accept tips directly. If a guest offers a tip where this is the policy, thank them and kindly explain the policy.
Check every bill for mistakes before you give it to the guest. Own up and correct any mistake straight away.

blocks.p: Every guest is different. Good service means noticing what each guest needs and adjusting, without making a fuss or making assumptions. When in doubt, **ask** politely: 'How may I help?'

head: Guest
What helps
rows: Families with babies and young children
Offer a high chair, cot, baby-changing area and child-friendly food
A quick check-in after a long journey
Safety: pool fences, window locks, hot items out of reach
A guest who is blind or has low vision
Ask if and how they would like help; do not grab their arm
Speak to the guest, not only to their companion
Read the menu aloud and say where things are on the table
Describe the layout, steps and hazards; do not move things without telling them
A guest who uses a wheelchair or has difficulty walking
Check **accessibility**: ramps, wide doors, an accessible bathroom, level paths
Offer a seat; ask before pushing a wheelchair
Do not lean on the chair or talk over the guest
A guest who is deaf or hard of hearing
Face the guest, speak clearly (not louder), and write things down
Get the guest's attention politely
A guest who speaks little English
Speak slowly in simple words; use gestures, pictures and a translation app
Write down prices and times; confirm in writing
Never shout
A guest with a food allergy, or who does not eat certain foods for health, religion or belief
Take it seriously; check with the chef before the guest orders
Never say a dish is 'probably fine'
Do not ask the guest to explain their religion
A VIP
Give extra care and follow the property's VIP procedures
Respect privacy: do not tell others who they are, and do not take photos without permission
An elderly guest
Offer a seat, patience, and help with luggage and stairs, with respect and without talking down

blocks.note: Treat a guest with a disability as you would any guest: with respect, and talk directly to them. Offer help but do not assume that they need it. The guest knows best what help they need.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Every guest gets the same standard of care, whatever their tip, nationality, age, appearance or religion.
Never joke about a guest's culture, accent, disability or religion. Never comment on their private life.
Keep guests' names, room numbers, health details and personal information **private**. Do not tell visitors, other guests or friends who is staying or what they said or did.

blocks.p: Even good properties make mistakes. What matters is what you do next. Handling a complaint well can turn an unhappy guest into a loyal one. This is called **service recovery**: putting things right after the service has gone wrong, so that the guest still leaves happy.

flow: Stay calm and listen to the whole story, without interrupting
Do not take it personally
Apologise sincerely, without blaming anyone
Show you understand how the guest feels
Fix what you can, quickly, within your authority
Pass on what you cannot fix, and tell the guest what will happen and when
Follow up to check the guest is satisfied
Report the cause so it does not happen again

head: Do
Do not
rows: Say 'I'm sorry this happened, and I will put it right.'
Argue, interrupt or make excuses
Take ownership: 'I will deal with this.'
Blame the kitchen, housekeeping, the driver or the guest
Offer a cold drink, a seat or a quick replacement
Say 'that's not my department' or 'there is nothing I can do'
Ask your supervisor about refunds, free items or room changes
Promise a refund, a free meal or an upgrade you cannot authorise
Keep the guest informed and check later
Leave the guest waiting without news

blocks.p: Example: a guest's airport pick-up did not arrive, so she took a taxi and arrived late, hot and upset. You greet her at once, listen, apologise, offer a cold drink and help with her bags, get her room ready, tell your supervisor, ask whether the taxi fare can be refunded (you cannot decide that), tell her what will happen, check later that she has settled in, and report the missed pick-up so it is investigated.

ul: Many travellers read **online reviews** and social media before they book. Good reviews bring guests at no cost; a few poor reviews can send them elsewhere. Reviews last a long time and can be read around the world.
Staff earn good reviews by giving warm, steady service to every guest, keeping the property clean, serving on time, giving honest advice and fixing problems **before the guest leaves**.
Pass on **praise** as well as complaints to your supervisor. Praise shows what works, so that it is kept up.

The manager or an authorised person replies to reviews: thanks the guest, apologises where needed and says what is being done. Staff must not argue online, ask friends to post false reviews, or post guests' private details or photos.
Feedback forms and comment cards tell the property what to improve. Encourage guests to fill them in.

blocks.p: A guest sees one business, not separate departments. So information must flow between them.

head: Department
How it helps the guest
What it must tell others
rows: Front office
Takes bookings and special requests; checks in and out
Arrivals, special requests, allergies, VIPs
Housekeeping
Has rooms clean and ready by check-in time
When each room is ready; maintenance faults; lost property
Kitchen and restaurant
Prepare and serve food safely and on time
Allergies, dishes that run out, long waits
Maintenance
Fixes faults quickly
When a repair is finished

ul: Use clear messages, a log book and proper handovers.
Help co-workers at busy times, and be polite when you ask for help.
Never say 'it is not my job' to a guest. Find the right person, make sure the guest is helped, and follow up.

blocks.p: **Harassment** of visitors means pestering them: following them, pressing them to buy, or not taking no for an answer. It makes visitors feel unsafe and unhappy. They may stay in their rooms, spend less, write poor reviews and tell friends not to come. This harms tourism, the jobs it brings and Jamaica's good name.

ul: Greet visitors warmly, give honest information, and recommend only licensed vendors, guides and taxis.
If you see a visitor being pestered, step in politely, guide the visitor away and call security or the supervisor. Do not argue or fight.
Know the rules of the property and area, and report problems that keep happening.
Never tell a guest that something is safe when it is not. A guest asks about swimming and the sea has strong currents: warn them and suggest a safer spot.
Never take shortcuts that put guests at risk: check that a high chair or cot is steady, keep walkways dry, and report faulty items.
Keep guests' privacy. A guest who asks you to keep their stay private must be respected.

blocks.note: Know the emergency numbers: 119 for police and 110 for fire and ambulance. Know where the first aid box and the nearest exits are, and know who the first aider is.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: I can explain the difference between product and service, and what guests expect and need.
I can say why customer service matters to guests, the business, me and Jamaica.
I can explain what front-line staff, moments of truth and internal customers are.
I can show good grooming, posture and attitude.
I can speak to guests with their titles and surnames, in a warm tone, using positive language.
I can greet, listen, ask open questions and give clear information face to face.
I can answer the telephone and write an email reply properly.
I can describe good service at each stage of the guest cycle.
I can anticipate a guest's need and exceed expectations within my limits.
I can share product and local knowledge, and recommend licensed operators honestly.
I can explain bills, GCT, exchange rates and the tipping policy.
I can serve guests with different needs: families, disabilities, language, diet and beliefs.
I can handle a complaint with service recovery and follow it up.
I can explain how online reviews affect a business and how staff help to earn good ones.
I can work with other departments and protect visitors and their privacy.

terms: How you treat the guests your business serves.
Staff who deal with guests face to face.
A co-worker or another department that depends on your work.
What a guest thinks the service will be like.
Each moment a guest has contact with the business and forms an opinion of it.
Happy guests telling family and friends about a business.
The stages from booking to arrival, the stay, departure and afterwards.
A cool drink given to guests as they arrive.
A record of a guest's past stays and likes.
Notice a need and meet it before the guest asks.
The staff member who helps guests with tours, taxis, restaurants and local information.
A guest who is very important to the business and given special attention.
Making a place easy for everyone to reach and use.
Putting things right after service has gone wrong.
Politely suggesting extras that suit the guest.
Pestering visitors so that they feel unsafe or unhappy.
Tourism Product Development Company, which runs Team Jamaica training.
A guest who has a booking but does not arrive and does not cancel.
The time by which guests must leave their room on the last day.

c1.title: A busy front desk in Negril
c1.text: Shelly is at the front desk of a small hotel in Negril, finishing a telephone booking. Mr and Mrs Grant, an elderly couple from Toronto, arrive at the desk. Mrs Grant uses a walking frame and looks tired after a long journey. Shelly knows their names from the booking list. Mr Grant asks what time the restaurant opens for dinner, which Shelly does not know, because it changed last week.

c2.title: Overcooked fish in Treasure Beach
c2.text: At a beach restaurant in Treasure Beach, a guest, Ms Hall, tells her server, Devon, that the grilled fish she ordered is dry and overcooked. She is hungry, her friends have almost finished eating, and she says in a loud voice that she will never come back. Devon is not sure whether he is allowed to take the dish off the bill. The manager, Mr Anderson, is in the office.

c3.title: Guests with different needs at a villa in Ocho Rios
c3.text: A villa in Ocho Rios welcomes three guests on the same day. Mr Thompson uses a wheelchair. Señora Ruiz speaks very little English. Mrs Dawkins is 82 and hard of hearing. Winston, the villa attendant, is showing each of them around the property, which has some steps at the pool and a ramp at the main entrance.

c4.title: The tour desk at a resort in St Ann
c4.text: At a mock tour desk in a resort in St Ann, Ayana is helping a family who want a river tour. The tour operator, who is licensed, says children must be at least 8 years old. The family has an 11-year-old and a 6-year-old. The father asks the price in US dollars and what is included. Ayana has the fact sheet but cannot see the lunch menu on it.

c5.title: Teamwork in a hotel kitchen in Montego Bay
c5.text: At a hotel in Montego Bay, the server Trevor keeps asking the kitchen to hurry. The cook, Mrs Brown, says that Trevor often forgets to tell her about allergies until the plate is nearly ready. Trevor says that guests keep complaining that they wait too long. A guest writes a praise card for Trevor's friendliness and for Mrs Brown's cooking.

questions.q: Shelly is finishing a call when the Grants reach the desk. What should she do?
o: Smile, make eye contact and show with a gesture that she will be with them shortly
Carry on with her call and give them her full attention only when she has finished
Cut the call short at once and ask the caller to phone back at a more convenient time
Ask the Grants to take a seat and wait for a member of staff to come to them
questions.why: A guest should never feel ignored. Acknowledging them with a smile and a gesture, and finishing the call politely and quickly, shows respect. Hanging up on a caller is also poor service.

questions.q: Mrs Grant uses a walking frame. What is the best way to help?
o: Offer her a seat, and ask her how she would like to be helped
Take her arm and walk her to the lift without asking her anything first
Ask Mr Grant what his wife can and cannot do, and speak only to him from then on
Say nothing about it, in case she is offended, and continue with the check-in
questions.why: Offer help but do not assume what is needed. Ask the guest directly and speak to her, not only to her husband. Doing nothing leaves a tired guest standing.

questions.q: How should Shelly address the Grants when she starts the check-in?
o: As 'Mr and Mrs Grant', which shows respect and shows she knows who they are
As 'Darling' and 'Sweetheart', to make an older couple feel at home in Jamaica
As 'Room 12', to save time because she has the booking list in front of her
By their first names, so they can feel relaxed at once after their long flight
questions.why: Use title and surname for guests once you know their names. Pet names, room numbers and first names without permission are too familiar or impersonal.

questions.q: Mr Grant asks what time dinner starts, and Shelly does not know. What should she say?
o: 'Let me find out for you', then check with the restaurant and come straight back
'I think it is about seven, but you could go and check at the restaurant yourself'
'You can find out from the menu in your room when you get there tonight'
'It is probably the same as last week, so I would just try and see what happens'
questions.why: Never guess, as a wrong answer wastes the guest's time. Say you will find out, check, and return quickly. Hotels keep information sheets for this reason.

questions.q: What should Devon do first when Ms Hall complains?
o: Listen to the whole complaint, apologise sincerely, and say he will put it right
Explain that the fish was cooked as the guest ordered and the kitchen followed the recipe
Ask her to lower her voice, because other guests can hear what she is saying
Tell her that complaints must be made to the manager in the office, not to the server
questions.why: The first steps in service recovery are to listen and apologise without arguing. Explaining or asking her to be quiet makes an upset guest feel unheard.

questions.q: Devon is not sure he can take the dish off the bill. What is the right action?
o: Offer to replace the fish quickly, and ask Mr Anderson about the bill
Take the dish off the bill himself, so that the guest is happy as soon as possible
Tell the guest that she must pay for it, since the cook cannot cook another one
Leave the dish on the table until someone else comes to see what the problem is
questions.why: Fix what is within your role, such as a fast replacement, and pass anything about charges to the supervisor, who has the authority to decide. Do not promise or refuse what you cannot decide.

questions.q: Ms Hall says in a loud voice that she will never come back. How should Devon take this?
o: Not personally: she is upset about the meal, so he stays calm and polite
As an insult to him, and he should show that he does not like being spoken to that way
As proof that she is a difficult guest, so that he should avoid her table from then on
As a sign that nothing can be done, so that he should leave the matter to the manager
questions.why: Guests are usually upset at the situation, not at the server. Staying calm and polite keeps the problem from growing and gives you the chance to recover the service.

questions.q: After the replacement fish is served, what should Devon do?
o: Check later that she is satisfied, and tell Mr Anderson so the cause is looked at
Assume that the problem is solved and avoid her table so that she is not disturbed again
Tell the cook that the guest complained, and that the cook should be more careful
Forget the matter, since the guest has a new meal and that was all she wanted
questions.why: Following up shows care, and reporting the cause helps the kitchen to prevent it. Blaming the cook or ignoring the matter means the same mistake can happen again.

questions.q: Winston is showing Mr Thompson the villa. Which action is best?
o: Ask where he would like help, and point out the ramp and the pool steps
Push the wheelchair around the property at once, so that he does not need to do anything
Take him only to places without steps, and not mention the parts that he cannot reach
Speak to his companion about what he needs, and leave it to her to explain to him
questions.why: Ask the guest what help he wants and give honest information about access. Pushing without asking, or hiding parts of the property, takes away his choice. Speak to the guest directly.

questions.q: Señora Ruiz speaks very little English. What is the best way to help her?
o: Speak slowly in simple words, use gestures and an app, and write down times and prices
Speak louder so that she can hear each word clearly, and repeat the sentence several times
Ask a co-worker to take over, and tell her to come back when someone speaks Spanish
Give her the full house-rules sheet in English, and ask her to read it in her room
questions.why: Language difficulty is not a hearing problem, so shouting does not help. Simple words, gestures, a translation app and written information make her feel welcome and informed.

questions.q: Mrs Dawkins is hard of hearing. How should Winston speak to her?
o: Face her, speak clearly at a normal pace, and write down anything important
Shout directly at her from across the patio, so that she can hear him wherever she is
Speak to her daughter, who is staying with her, instead of speaking to Mrs Dawkins herself
Talk very quickly so that the explanation is finished before she gets tired of listening
questions.why: Facing the guest helps her see your lips and face, and a clear, steady voice is better than a loud one. Writing down key information, and speaking to the guest herself, shows respect.

questions.q: Why should Winston give the same standard of care to all three guests?
o: Every guest deserves the same respect, whatever their needs, nationality, age or tip
Because guests with special needs usually give the largest tips to the staff of the villa
Because the manager will check which guest Winston spends the longest time with
Because it is the only way to be sure that none of them will write a review online
questions.why: Fair, respectful service is a principle, not a trade for tips or reviews. Every guest should feel equally welcome and valued.

questions.q: The family has a 6-year-old and the tour has an age limit of 8. What should Ayana say?
o: Explain the age rule kindly, and suggest an activity that the whole family can do together
Say it will probably be fine, since the 6-year-old looks tall for his age and could join in
Tell them the tour is cancelled today, to avoid explaining the age rule to the family
Suggest that the 11-year-old and the parents go, and leave the 6-year-old with another guest
questions.why: Age limits are set for safety, so Ayana must be honest and not bend them. Offering an alternative that suits the family keeps the service positive.

questions.q: Ayana cannot see the lunch menu on the fact sheet. What should she do?
o: Say she will check with the tour operator, and give the guest the answer as soon as she has it
Tell the guest that lunch is probably included, since most tours include a meal
Tell the guest she does not have that information, and that he should ask the operator himself
List a menu from another tour she remembers, so that the guest has something to decide on
questions.why: Never guess about what is included or about prices. Finding out, and coming back quickly, is good service. Sending the guest away or inventing details makes the property look unprepared.

questions.q: The father asks for the price in US dollars. Which is correct?
o: Give the price exactly as shown on the fact pack, and show it in writing
Work it out from the J$ price using a rate she saw on the news this morning
Round the price up or down to a figure that is easier for the family to remember
Tell the family she cannot give prices, and that the operator will tell them tomorrow
questions.why: Use the prices set by the property and written in the fact pack. Using your own exchange rate, or rounding, can cause an argument or a loss, and refusing to give prices is unhelpful.

questions.q: What is the best way for Ayana to confirm the booking?
o: Repeat the tour, date, pick-up and price to the father, and confirm in writing
Tell the father that the tour is booked, and trust the family to remember the details
Write the booking in her notebook, and let the tour operator contact them nearer the time
Ask the father to remind her of the booking the evening before the tour takes place
questions.why: Repeating details back and confirming in writing avoids misunderstandings about the date, the pick-up time or the price. Relying on memory or on guests to remind you leads to missed tours.

questions.q: What is the best way for Trevor to help the kitchen serve guests faster?
o: Tell Mrs Brown about allergies and special requests when he enters the order
Go into the kitchen and ask for the plate to be rushed each time a table is late
Tell the guests that the kitchen is short of staff and that nobody can speed it up
Enter orders in groups at the end of the round, so that the cook receives fewer slips
questions.why: Clear and early information is how internal customers help each other. The kitchen can plan allergies and times when it knows early, and delays often start with late or missing information.

questions.q: What does the term 'internal customer' mean in this situation?
o: Mrs Brown, whose work depends on Trevor's information, as his does on hers
A guest who stays at the hotel for several weeks and uses all of its services
A guest who is writing a comment card for the hotel's own records
The hotel manager, who is the only person that the staff must please
questions.why: Co-workers and departments that depend on your work are your internal customers. Good service to them makes good service to guests possible.

questions.q: What should the supervisor do with the guest's praise card?
o: Share it with Trevor and Mrs Brown, so they know what works and keep it up
File it, because praise is not as important as complaints and needs no action
Show it only to Trevor, because the server is the one who talks to the guest
Hand it to the manager and ask whether either of them should be paid extra
questions.why: Sharing praise shows the whole team what works and motivates them. It should go to everyone who earned it, not only the person the guest met.

questions.q: A guest at the villa asks you why the Wi-Fi is not working. It is not your department. What should you do?
o: Apologise, find out who can fix it, tell the guest what will happen, and check later
Tell the guest it is not your department and that she should ask at the front desk
Tell the guest that Wi-Fi is often slow in Jamaica and she should not expect too much
Switch the router off and on yourself, even though you have not been shown how to do it
questions.why: Never say 'it is not my job'. Take ownership of the guest's problem, pass it to the right person, tell the guest what will happen and follow up. Do not tamper with equipment you have not been trained to handle.
